specPoints.text: CORE PRACTICAL 8 Analysis of some inorganic and organic unknowns.

primer.text: Unknown ions confess under the right witnesses. This note runs the ammonium, carbonate and sulfate test-tube reactions with their ionic equations and observations, then turns to the flame, where a cleaned wire and a single ion paint the colour that names the metal.

lessons.title: Test-tube identification and the ammonium test
lessons.opening: Core Practical 8 identifies unknown ions with nothing but test tubes and reagents. The ion menu covers ammonium, halides, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates and sulfates, and the ammonium test pairs sodium hydroxide with warm, damp red litmus that turns blue in ammonia's presence.
keyPoints: Simple test-tube reactions identify ammonium, halide, carbonate, hydrogencarbonate and sulfate ions.
Solid samples are dissolved in deionised water before testing.
The ammonium test adds sodium hydroxide to the sample and warms it gently in a water bath.
Ammonia gas is released, and damp red litmus paper held at the tube mouth turns blue.
The ionic equation is NH4+ plus OH- giving NH3 and water.

low.restatement: Dissolve the solid, add alkali, warm the tube in a water bath and hold damp red litmus at the mouth: blue litmus certifies ammonium ions through the ammonia they release.
low.analogy: A handshake you can smell: the alkali squeezes ammonia out of the ammonium ion, and the litmus paper is the sniff-test witness that changes colour.
low.examPointer: State both the overall and ionic equations, and specify damp red litmus, not any paper, when writing the method.

medium.restatement: The alkali converts ammonium ions into ammonia molecules; warming drives the gas out of solution, and ammonia's basicity is what flips the damp red litmus to blue - the moisture on the paper lets the gas dissolve and act.
medium.analogy: Persuading a shy guest out of a room: the alkali nudges the ammonium ion, the warm bath opens the exit, and the litmus greets the guest in the doorway.
medium.examPointer: Explain the dampness requirement - dry paper cannot dissolve the ammonia, so the colour change needs the wet surface.

check.stem: Before testing a solid unknown, the sample must be

options.text: Dissolved in deionised water to make an aqueous solution
options.explanation: The test-tube reactions run on aqueous samples, so solids are dissolved first.

options.text: Heated until it melts
options.explanation: Melting is not part of the test preparation.

options.text: Ground into a powder and tested dry
options.explanation: Dry solids do not undergo the ionic tests.

options.text: Mixed with ethanol
options.explanation: Ethanol appears in the hydrolysis practical, not this one.

check.stem: Which observation confirms ammonium ions in the test tube?

options.text: Damp red litmus paper held at the tube mouth turns blue on warming
options.explanation: The ammonia released is basic enough to flip the damp red litmus.

options.text: A white precipitate forms immediately
options.explanation: White precipitates belong to chloride and sulfate tests.

options.text: The limewater turns milky
options.explanation: That is the carbonate test's sign.

options.text: A brick-red precipitate appears
options.explanation: That belongs to Fehling's solution chemistry.

check.stem: Why is the test tube warmed gently in a water bath?

options.text: To drive the ammonia gas out of solution so it reaches the litmus paper
options.explanation: Warmth releases the dissolved ammonia to the tube mouth.

options.text: To speed up the dissolution of the solid sample
options.explanation: The sample is already dissolved by this stage.

options.text: To evaporate the sodium hydroxide
options.explanation: Evaporating the reagent would spoil the test.

options.text: Because ammonia only turns litmus blue when heated
options.explanation: Ammonia's basicity does the colour change; warmth just delivers the gas.

check.stem: The ionic equation for the ammonium test is

options.text: NH4+ plus OH- gives NH3 and H2O
options.explanation: The ammonium ion loses a proton to hydroxide, forming ammonia and water.

options.text: NH4+ plus H+ gives NH3 and water
options.explanation: The reagent supplies hydroxide, not protons.

options.text: 2H+ plus CO3 2- gives CO2 and H2O
options.explanation: That is the carbonate test's ionic equation.

options.text: Ba 2+ plus SO4 2- gives BaSO4
options.explanation: That is the sulfate test's equation.

check.stem: Which ions are identified by simple test-tube reactions in this practical?

options.text: Ammonium, halide, carbonate, hydrogencarbonate and sulfate ions
options.explanation: The menu spans the five ionic species the tests cover.

options.text: Transition metal ions only
options.explanation: Flame tests appear later in the note, but the test-tube menu is the five above.

options.text: Only chloride ions
options.explanation: The menu is far wider than one halide.

options.text: Organic functional groups only
options.explanation: The named tests target inorganic ions.

check.stem: State the overall equation for the ammonium test with ammonium chloride.
check.modelAnswer: NH4Cl + NaOH gives NH3 + H2O + NaCl, releasing ammonia gas.

check.stem: State the litmus condition that the ammonium test requires.
check.modelAnswer: Damp red litmus paper is held near the tube mouth and turns blue in the ammonia fumes.

check.stem: Explain why the litmus paper must be damp for the ammonium test to work.
check.modelAnswer: Ammonia must dissolve on the paper to exert its basic effect, and only a damp surface provides the water that converts the gas into the alkaline solution that turns the litmus blue.

check.stem: A student performs the ammonium test with dry blue litmus and sees nothing. Identify the fault and state the corrected procedure.
check.modelAnswer: Dry paper cannot dissolve the ammonia, so the test fails; the correction is damp red litmus held at the tube mouth of the gently warmed mixture, which turns blue.

lessons.title: Carbonate and sulfate tests
lessons.opening: Carbonates announce themselves with fizzing and milky limewater, sulfates with a white barium precipitate. This lesson writes both ionic equations, runs the delivery-tube set-up for the carbon dioxide, and explains why acid comes first in the sulfate test.
keyPoints: Carbonate ions react with acid to release carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.
The carbonate ionic equation is 2H+ plus CO3 2- giving CO2 and H2O; hydrogencarbonate releases the same gas one proton at a time.
The delivery tube carries the gas into a second tube holding limewater, calcium hydroxide solution.
Sulfate ions with acidified barium chloride give a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
Hydrochloric acid is added first in the sulfate test to remove carbonates that would otherwise precipitate and confuse the result.

low.restatement: Add acid to the unknown: fizzing plus milky limewater convicts a carbonate; for sulfates, acidify first, then add barium chloride and read the white precipitate as the verdict.
low.analogy: Carbonates confess loudly by bubbling; sulfates need their own witness, the barium, and the acid clears the courtroom of carbonate impostors first.
low.examPointer: Write both ionic equations and state the acid-first rule with its reason when explaining the sulfate method.

medium.restatement: The limewater verdict is a precipitation chain: carbon dioxide converts calcium hydroxide solution into insoluble calcium carbonate, hence the milkiness; in the sulfate test the acid pre-treatment eliminates carbonate ions that would also form white barium carbonate, so any white precipitate that remains is sulfate's own.
medium.analogy: An alibi check: the acid removes the suspect (carbonate) whose fingerprints would match the crime scene's white powder, leaving sulfate with no cover.
medium.examPointer: Quote both the carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ionic equations, noting the proton ratio difference.

check.stem: What turns limewater milky in the carbonate test?

options.text: Carbon dioxide reacting to form insoluble calcium carbonate
options.explanation: The gas converts dissolved calcium hydroxide into a white suspended solid.

options.text: Hydrogen gas bubbling through
options.explanation: Hydrogen does not react with limewater.

options.text: Dissolved sodium carbonate carried over
options.explanation: The test isolates the gas; the solution stays behind.

options.text: Oxygen from the air dissolving in the limewater
options.explanation: Air exposure is not the reaction's driver.

check.stem: The ionic equation for the carbonate test is

options.text: 2H+ plus CO3 2- gives CO2 plus H2O
options.explanation: Two protons neutralise one carbonate ion to the gas and water.

options.text: H+ plus CO3 2- gives HCO3-
options.explanation: That is the first protonation step, not the test's net outcome.

options.text: NH4+ plus OH- gives NH3 plus H2O
options.explanation: That is the ammonium equation.

options.text: Ag+ plus Cl- gives AgCl
options.explanation: That is a halide-test equation.

check.stem: Why is dilute hydrochloric acid added before barium chloride in the sulfate test?

options.text: To remove carbonate ions that would also form a white precipitate and falsely mimic sulfate
options.explanation: The acid eliminates the carbonate interference before the barium reads the sample.

options.text: To dissolve the barium chloride faster
options.explanation: The barium chloride dissolves readily on its own.

options.text: To turn the solution acidic for colour detection
options.explanation: The test reads a precipitate, not a colour.

options.text: Because barium chloride only works in acid
options.explanation: Barium ions precipitate sulfate regardless; the acid guards against carbonates.

check.stem: The white precipitate in a positive sulfate test is

options.text: Barium sulfate, BaSO4
options.explanation: Barium ions and sulfate ions combine into the insoluble white solid.

options.text: Barium carbonate
options.explanation: Barium carbonate would indicate the removed carbonate interference, not the sulfate verdict.

options.text: Calcium carbonate
options.explanation: That belongs to the limewater reaction.

options.text: Silver chloride
options.explanation: That belongs to halide testing.

check.stem: Sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts with acid differently from sodium carbonate in that

options.text: One proton reacts per hydrogencarbonate ion, where carbonate needs two
options.explanation: The ionic equations show H+ plus HCO3- against 2H+ plus CO3 2-.

options.text: It releases no carbon dioxide at all
options.explanation: Hydrogencarbonate releases the same carbon dioxide gas.

options.text: It turns limewater blue instead of milky
options.explanation: Limewater's response is the same milkiness.

options.text: It needs no acid to react
options.explanation: The acid drives both reactions.

check.stem: State the delivery set-up used in the carbonate test.
check.modelAnswer: A bung with a delivery tube carries the evolved gas into a second tube containing limewater.

check.stem: Write the ionic equation for the sulfate test.
check.modelAnswer: Ba 2+ plus SO4 2- gives BaSO4, the white precipitate.

check.stem: Explain why the carbonate interference in the sulfate test is decisive enough to require the acid-first step.
check.modelAnswer: Barium carbonate is also a white precipitate, so a sample containing carbonate ions would mimic the sulfate result exactly; the acid-first step destroys the carbonates before barium is introduced, reserving the white precipitate for sulfate alone.

check.stem: An unknown solution fizzes with acid and its gas turns limewater milky. State the ion identified and write the ionic equation for the fizzing.
check.modelAnswer: Carbonate ions are present, and the fizzing follows the ionic equation 2H+ plus CO3 2- giving CO2 and H2O.

lessons.title: Flame tests for metal ions
lessons.opening: Metal ions paint a Bunsen flame in their signature colours. The technique is small: clean the wire until it shows no colour, touch the sample, and read the flame's edge. Cleanliness is everything, because a contaminated wire mixes colours and misleads the identification.
keyPoints: Metal ions heated strongly in a flame emit characteristic colours that identify them.
The nichrome or platinum wire loop is dipped in concentrated acid and held in the blue flame until no colour shows, cleaning it.
Cleaning prevents contamination, since mixed ions give mixed colours and ruin the identification.
The sample is held at the edge of the blue flame, avoiding letting the wire glow red-hot.
Each metal ion carries its own flame colour, listed in the flame-test colour table.

low.restatement: Acid-dip the wire, burn it clean, load a trace of sample, and hold it at the flame's edge: the colour that blooms there names the metal ion, provided no stray ion shares the stage.
low.analogy: A spotlight on a solo performer: any leftover performer from the previous act blends costumes and confuses the audience, so the stage is cleared first.
low.examPointer: Describe the cleaning step and the glow-red avoidance when writing the flame-test method.

medium.restatement: The emission is atomic: heat promotes electrons in the metal ion, and the light they emit falling back is the element's optical fingerprint; two metals together superimpose their fingerprints, which is why a single-ion sample is the method's precondition.
medium.analogy: Two radios on one frequency broadcast a jumble; one metal ion per flame keeps the broadcast clean.
medium.examPointer: Explain contamination as mixed emissions rather than a chemical reaction between the ions.

check.stem: The wire loop is cleaned by dipping in concentrated acid and heating until no colour shows in order to

options.text: Remove any previous sample so only one ion type colours the flame
options.explanation: A clean wire guarantees the observed colour belongs to the unknown alone.

options.text: Sterilise the wire against bacteria
options.explanation: Sterility is irrelevant to the emission test.

options.text: Coat the wire with acid to brighten the flame
options.explanation: The acid cleans; it does not brighten anything.

options.text: Make the wire more conductive
options.explanation: Conductivity plays no role in flame emission.

check.stem: Why does a wire glowing red-hot confuse the flame colour reading?

options.text: The red glow of hot wire can be confused with a genuine flame colour
options.explanation: Self-emission from hot metal would masquerade as the sample's colour.

options.text: The wire would melt at that temperature
options.explanation: Nichrome survives far beyond a red glow.

options.text: The sample would evaporate completely
options.explanation: Some volatilisation is normal; the confusion concern is the glow.

options.text: Red light indicates a failed test
options.explanation: The concern is misleading colour, not pass-fail signalling.

check.stem: Flame tests identify metal ions because

options.text: Each metal ion emits its own characteristic colour when heated strongly
options.explanation: The element's electronic structure sets its emission fingerprint.

options.text: Every metal burns with the same colour
options.explanation: Distinct colours are the method's entire basis.

options.text: The acid changes colour with each metal
options.explanation: The acid is the cleaner, not the indicator.

options.text: The Bunsen flame itself changes with the metal
options.explanation: The flame's blue cone stays; the colour comes from the ion.

check.stem: Two metal ions heated on the same wire produce what flame outcome?

options.text: Mixed colours that make identification erroneous
options.explanation: Superimposed emissions blur the signature the method relies on.

options.text: A new, third colour unique to the mixture
options.explanation: The emissions add, they do not chemically react into a new colour.

options.text: No colour at all
options.explanation: Both ions still emit; the result is a jumble, not silence.

options.text: The colour of whichever ion is heavier
options.explanation: Emission depends on electronic structure, not mass.

check.stem: Where in the flame should the loaded wire be held?

options.text: At the edge of the blue Bunsen flame
options.explanation: The edge gives the strong, readable emission zone.

options.text: Deep inside the blue cone
options.explanation: The hot cone is for cleaning, not sampling.

options.text: Above the flame entirely, in the air
options.explanation: Above the flame the sample receives no heat.

options.text: Touching the burner barrel
options.explanation: That heats the wire without sampling properly.

check.stem: State the two wire materials used for flame tests.
check.modelAnswer: Unreactive metal wires such as nichrome or platinum are used for the loop.

check.stem: State the precondition that makes a flame colour readable.
check.modelAnswer: The test works only when a single type of ion is present, which is why the wire is cleaned until it shows no colour.

check.stem: Explain why the flame test cannot reliably identify a mixture of two metal ions.
check.modelAnswer: Each ion emits its own colour simultaneously, and the superimposed emissions blend in the flame, so the observed colour no longer matches either ion's clean signature and the identification becomes erroneous.

check.stem: A wire shows a persistent yellow flame even after one acid dip. Suggest the fault and the corrective action before running the unknown test.
check.modelAnswer: Residual contamination, most commonly sodium, still colours the flame; the corrective action is repeating the acid-dip-and-burn cycle until the flame shows no colour at all, then loading the unknown.

glossary.definition: Calcium hydroxide solution that turns milky with carbon dioxide as insoluble calcium carbonate forms.
Identification of a metal ion by the characteristic colour it emits in a hot Bunsen flame.
The equation showing only the reacting ions, such as the carbonate or sulfate test equations.
